Abstract Renewable electricity, production/storage and distribution of green hydrogen and carbon dioxide emission reduction are just three of the practices needed for a net zero-emission world. The increasing amount of renewable energy produced requires the development of versatile technologies capable to store the excess renewable electricity produced. Hydrogen production through electrolysis, despite not being still economically viable, can be considered a mature technology. Different strategies to convert H2 into more volumetric dense fuel are under development through Power-to-Chemicals (PtC) process. Among these, CO2 methanation offers the advantage of a wide infrastructure available for the distribution and use of methane as chemical and fuel for both heat and power generation. The latter approach is also called Power-to-Gas (PtG) process. These technologies in the last year have been the focus of research, both public and private. In particular, direct methanation of biogas obtained from anaerobic digestors represents a challenge and an interesting opportunity due to the possibility to avoid the CO2 separation step at the moment needed for biogas purification to biomethane. Since CO2 separation is an additional cost, this route can be the key for economic sustainability of the process. In this review we focus on the main aspects involved in the design of a methanation plant, with a particular focus on the biogas methanation, starting from the reaction thermodynamics and kinetics. Afterwards, light is shed on the most interesting catalysts reported in the literature, with a focus on Ni-based catalysts and considering the support role in the reaction. Different kinetic approaches currently available and promising reactor types, including different simulation models, which are becoming increasingly fundamental in the reactor design and scale-up phase, are reported. Climate change, fossil fuel, carbon dioxide emissions, environmental issues are just some of the words that in the lasts years have played a significant part in public opinion and debate (Calculli et al., 2021). World researchers are confident that anthropogenic emissions are the main cause of global warming and the development of technologies able to reduce CO2 footprint has been favored by economic incentives such as CO2 tax credit (Lee et al., 2019, Tan et al., 2022, Krishfield et al., 2021). The driving force towards a sustainable transition has never been so strong and this opens the road to the development of alternative synthesis of chemical and fuels. Green hydrogen, photocatalysis, photoelectrocatalysis, ammonia production, power to gas and power to liquids are just some of the main research lines that are currently being investigated. Renewable electricity, batteries, hydrogen and carbon dioxide emission reduction are the four key-words for a net zero-emission world. Estimation states that in order to stay below the 2 °C increase in the world temperature, a reduction of 75/50% of global greenhouse gas input into the atmosphere by 2050 is needed (Bataille et al., 2021). Unfortunately at the moment we are still far from the net zero emission goal, with a CO2 concentration in the atmosphere which is about 420 ppm and is expected to rise up to 600–1550 ppm in the next decades (Leung et al., 2014). The use of carbon dioxide as a reactant will very likely play an important role in the near future. INTRODUCTION Currently with the growing environmental impact and cost of energy production via fossil fuels, interest is now growing in renewable energy. Carbon dioxide is the major greenhouse gas produced by combustion of various fossil fuels and has a major role in the increase in the temperature of the earth's atmosphere. In order to overcome this dilemma, there is a move towards low carbon emissions via the use of carbon-neutral fuels.1 Catalytic reactions of H2 and CO2 (hydrogenation) have been used to produce a range of useful fuels and chemicals, including, methane, gasoline range hydrocarbons, C2 C2 alkenes, organic acids, methanol and other alcohols.2 There is particular interest in the production of methane from the catalytic hydrogenation process, i.e. methanation (Reaction 1). 2,3 CO2 + 4H2 CH4 + 2H2 O (Methanation Reaction) (1) However, the mechanism of the CO2 methanation reaction remains unclear.4 Some studies have suggested the reverse water gas shift (RWGS) reaction (Reaction 2) as an intermediate reaction in the production of methane by CO2 hydrogenation. The produced CO from the RWGS reaction reacts with the H2 to produce methane (Reaction 3).5 Alternatively, some studies have assumed that the produced CO and CH4 are the product of two parallel reactions (1) and (2). CO2 + H2 CO + H2 O (RWGS Reaction) (2) CO + 3H2 CH4 + H2 O (3) It has been shown that the methanation reaction is dependent on several factors i.e. temperature, pressure, reactant gas composition (CO2: H2 ratio).6-8 For example, because the methanation reaction is exothermic, lower temperatures favors the reaction 6 and a typical operational temperature range for methane production is from 200 - 500 C 8,9. The H2/CO2 ratio in CO2 methanation controls the balance between CO2 conversion, methane formation, and side reactions by shifting the availability of hydrogen relative to carbon dioxide. Mechanistically, the review states that both CO2 conversion and CH4 selectivity are affected by the H2/CO2 ratio, with high values allowing high conversion and selectivity toward methane [N1-R1]. The thermodynamic and reaction-path discussion reinforces that methanation is exothermic, and higher pressures and lower temperatures favor the reaction, which is relevant because the H2/CO2 ratio indirectly affects stoichiometric and thermodynamic favorability by altering the effective H2 supply relative to CO2 [N4-R3]. The review also notes that the Sabatier reaction is the main strategy for converting pure captured CO2 to methane using green H2, and that catalyst supports and reaction conditions are key to optimizing this process [N4-R1].

At low H2/CO2 ratios, the system is less favorable for complete methane formation because there is insufficient hydrogen to fully reduce CO2. In contrast, higher H2/CO2 ratios provide more H2 relative to CO2, which supports higher CO2 conversion and methane yield, as shown in the experimental parametric study where a 4:1 H2:CO2 ratio gave higher CO2 conversion and high methane yield [N2-F2]. The same study also says that the methanation reaction is dependent on the CO2:H2 ratio, with lower temperatures favoring the reaction and higher pressures also improving conversion [N2-F2]. Thermodynamically consistent reaction mechanisms for CO and CO2 methanation over Ni-based catalysts further support the idea that H2 availability governs pathway preference and product distribution [N4-R2].

The ratio also limits selectivity toward methane versus side reactions. The review explicitly states that catalysts can enhance CH4 selectivity from CO2 methanation, and that heterogeneous VIII B group metal catalysts such as Ni, Fe, Co, Ru, Rh, Pt, Pd have been studied to optimize methane production [N4-R3]. The parametric study likewise shows that different catalyst supports and promoters can change the outcome: for example, the 10wt.%-Ni/Al2O3 catalyst was optimal for CO2 conversion and methane yield, but Fe and Co promoters reduced methane yield due to sintering and non-uniform metal dispersion [N2-F2]. This implies that the H2/CO2 ratio influences not only how much CO2 is converted but also how much of the product is selectively methane versus carbon monoxide, water, or other byproducts. The review also emphasizes that reactor design, catalyst supports, and reaction conditions are central to optimizing the process [N4-R3].

Overall, the H2/CO2 ratio controls the thermodynamic and kinetic accessibility of the Sabatier pathway, determines whether the system is H2-rich enough to support high conversion and selectivity, and sets the operating window where side reactions or catalyst deactivation become more significant [N1-R1][N4-R3][N4-R2].

This study also notes that the methanation reaction is dependent on temperature, pressure, and reactant gas composition, including the CO2:H2 ratio [N2-F2].

The review supports a broader pattern: both CO2 conversion and CH4 selectivity are affected by the H2/CO2 ratio, with high values allowing high conversion and selectivity toward methane [N1-R1]. The experimental study on Ni/Al2O3 and Ru-based catalysts under conditions of atmospheric pressure further indicates that catalyst choice matters, because the paper reports CO2 methanation performance using Ni/Al2O3, Ru/Al2O3, and Ru-Ni/Al2O3 [N6-R5]. In addition, the Ni/Al2O3 study shows that the feed gas used a H2:CO2 ratio of 4:1 with 10% CO2, 40% H2, and 50% Ar, and that the reaction conditions are carefully selected to match the stoichiometric methanation reaction [N6-R2]. This suggests that some experimental work actively tunes the ratio to achieve the desired stoichiometry, rather than simply varying it arbitrarily.

Catalyst and reactor conditions can amplify or suppress the effect of the H2/CO2 ratio. The parametric study shows that the best performance came with Ni/Al2O3 under optimized temperature, GHSV, and H2:CO2 ratio, while Fe and Co promoters reduced methane yield due to sintering and poor metal dispersion [N2-F2]. The review also notes that different supports and promoters have been studied extensively, with Ru, Rh, and Ni-based catalysts showing efficient catalytic activity and methane selectivity [N4-R3]. The review further emphasizes that reactor design and process optimization are key aspects of methanation plants [N4-R1].

There are exceptions and conflicts in the literature, but they are not strong enough to override the general trend. The main exception in the provided evidence is that the Ni/Al2O3 study reports a 24 wt% Ni/Al2O3 catalyst for hydrogenation of CO2 and CO to CH4, and that this catalyst was studied in mixed syngas with CO2 and CO [N2-R5]. This shows that the effect of H2/CO2 ratio can be studied in mixed feed systems, where the ratio is part of a broader syngas composition, not just pure CO2 and H2. However, the provided evidence does not report contradictory results across catalysts or operating windows; instead, it consistently supports a positive correlation between higher H2/CO2 ratios and better conversion and methane yield in the studies cited [N2-F2][N4-R3][N6-R2].

In short, the empirical trend is that higher H2/CO2 ratios improve CO2 conversion and methane yield, while catalysts and reactor conditions determine how strongly this effect is manifested [N2-F2][N1-R1][N4-R3].
